reading.body:
The AI Policy Network's five AI lobbying filings name twelve lobbyists and eighteen bills, a breadth that suggests AI policy work is now a standing portfolio rather than a single-issue campaign.

The lobbyist counts cluster: four lobbyists appear on all five filings, five appear on three, and three appear on one or two. That spread is consistent with a firm staffing a client continuously across a session rather than assembling a team for one bill. The bills named span both chambers and both "S" and "HR" prefixes, which means the firm is tracking AI legislation as it moves rather than anchoring to one vehicle.

For AI specifically, this is the policy layer that sits upstream of compute. Rules on model deployment, data, and liability are written before they reach the grid or the data center, and a firm filing on eighteen bills is positioned to shape that text. The filings do not say what positions were argued, only that AI was among the issues lobbied.

What the data does not cover: the substance of any filing, the amounts spent, the agencies contacted, or whether any bill advanced. It records presence on filings, not influence.
